summary: Defines a human-readable string format for LDAP search filters, which LDAP otherwise sends as network encodings, so applications can write filters in a common textual form. It was replaced by RFC 1960.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1558 defines a text form for LDAP search filters so applications and people can write searches in a readable way. It uses parentheses, prefix logical operators, and comparisons; RFC 1960 later obsoleted this memo.

subtitle: A readable string syntax for expressing LDAP search filters.

tldr.problem: LDAP search filters are encoded for network transmission, but applications may need a human-readable way to represent them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a parenthesized prefix syntax with logical operators, attribute comparisons, presence tests, and substring matching.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1558 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 1960.

today: RFC 1558 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 1960.

sections.title: From Network Encoding to Text
sections.content: LDAP defines a network representation of search filters. RFC 1558 provides a human-readable string format for applications that need a common text representation. The format uses prefix notation, placing a logical operator before its filters.
sections.plainLanguage: The network form of an LDAP search filter is not easy to read. This memo defines a text form that people and applications can use to express the same kind of search.

sections.title: Operators and Comparisons
sections.content: A filter is enclosed in parentheses. The logical operators are & for AND, | for OR, and ! for NOT. Simple comparisons use =, ~=, >=, or <=. The =* form tests whether an attribute is present. Substring filters use the asterisk as a wildcard, and an asterisk or parenthesis in a value is escaped with a backslash.
sections.plainLanguage: Put each filter in parentheses. Use ampersand for AND, a vertical bar for OR, and an exclamation mark for NOT; comparisons test an attribute against a value.

sections.title: Example Filter Strings
sections.content:
(cn=Babs Jensen) tests for a common name equal to Babs Jensen. (!(cn=Tim Howes)) negates that equality test. (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))) combines an AND with an OR. (o=univ*of*mich*) uses substring wildcards in an organization value.

The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters can combine conditions, negate a condition, or match part of an attribute value. The parentheses make the structure visible in the text.
